OPEN INNOVATION — CLASS TOPIC

What are Corporates Doing?

The class material compares examples involving P&G, LEGO, ISRO and PHILIPS.

The examples examine:
- Source of idea / innovation
- Whether the source is external or internal
- Direction of flow of knowledge or innovation
- Main actor initiating the move
- Purpose of the main actor
- Value for the corporate / main actor
- Value for the partner
- Ownership / control of knowledge

Examples discussed in the class material include:

P&G:
Source of idea / innovation: Outsiders / External
Direction of flow: Outside to Inside
Main actor initiating the move: Outsiders
Purpose mentioned in the class material includes increasing market reach.

LEGO:
Source of idea / innovation: Outsiders / External
Direction of flow: Outside to Inside
Main actor initiating the move: Outsiders
Purposes mentioned include revenue / profit and becoming more innovative.
Value mentioned includes validated ideas.

ISRO:
Source of idea / innovation: Internal / Inside
Direction of flow: Inside to outside
Purposes mentioned include reducing import dependence, private-sector participation, ecosystem building and generating revenue.

PHILIPS:
Source of idea / innovation: Internal / Inside
Direction of flow: Inside to outside
Purpose includes a marketing move, saving R&D time and cost, and validated ideas.
The material also refers to ownership / control of knowledge.

Value for partners discussed in the material includes:
- Brand recognition
- Global market access
- Revenues
- Saving R&D cost and time
- Access to advanced technology
- Access to customers

Knowledge Landscape:
The class material asks students to find examples for the next class.

Open Innovation Approaches:
The class material introduces open innovation approaches as a topic for discussion.

Background: 
Most academic programs focus on startups  OR corporates in isolation, leaving a critical gap in 
training students and professionals to visualize these two different kinds of important organizations 
working together for creating more impact . Bigger corporates interacting with startups might be 
seen as a paradox. However, the trend is reversing now and the more of these interactions are not 
for the sake of checklist completion. Corporate innovation literature finds many ways through 
which bigger established corporates can innovate and remain ahead of the curve. Co -creating the 
solutions with the startups is one of them. On the other hands startups feel that their size is not

solutions with the startups is one of them. On the other hands startups feel that their size is not 
relevant for the corporates, and they fear the failure of getting overshadowed by the big corporates. 
In this paradox lies various opportunities which can help the startups and the corporates to come 
together. There have been examples coming from Indian ecosystem where startups from their 
incubation stages have been able to forge partnership with big corporates. Examples such as 
BioNTech providing its technical knowledge on mRNA molecules while Pfizer bringing years of 
experience in manufacturing it on a large scale and distributing it to the world during Covid19. As 
the students graduate from their programs major natural outlets for them are ; working with the 
startups, starting their own ventures, or working with the bigger corporates. In all these scenarios 
it is very critical that they understand the relationship, opportunities, and various frameworks under

it is very critical that they understand the relationship, opportunities, and various frameworks under 
which an effective startup-corporate collaboration can work. Moreover, the existing courses being 
offered across BMU doesn’t offer it as a comprehensive package. The increasing importance and 
instances of more number of corporates working with the startups at the global level as well as in 
India makes it a right moment for us to introduce our students with these frameworks and examples 
from the ecosystem. 
Course Description: 
This course at the basic level will help the students to understand the need of the partnership 
between startups and the corporates. Why this is important beyond the current merger and 
acquisitions. Building on that understanding it will empower students to understand various 
models for these partnerships and defining features of these models. These models would be a

models for these partnerships and defining features of these models. These models would be a 
basket of options available to both the parties right from providing access to facilities to having 
majority equity stakes in those startups. Through a blend of Indian and global case studies  across 
sectors, hands-on projects, and interactive workshops, students will learn how to identify strategic 
value spaces, design win -win engagement models, and navigate cultural and operational 
challenges unique to such partnerships. The curriculum will cover the full collaboration lifecycle—

from opportunity mapping and venture vehicle selection to execution, risk management, and 
scaling innovation for mutual growth.  
The course is designed with the objective of introducing the students with key concepts and 
frameworks for corporate-startup collaboration. Why these collaborations are important. What are

collaboration. 
ii. Analyze challenges and success factors in corporate -startup partnerships using real-world 
cases. 
iii. Design a practical blueprint for an effective corporate -startup partnership for different 
context of innovation.

A. Industry Undercurrents: Where is the money? 
• Go to the GCV Powerlist 2025 website. (https://globalventuring.com/intelligence/2026-

What to do for each deal

interviews about the same deal. 
• Study all the material carefully. 
• Try to understand why the deal was done.

Entrepreneurship
Big Companies Should
Collaborate with Startups
by Eddie Yoon and Steve Hughes
February 25, 2016
Campbell, the food company best known for its soups, is investing
$125 million in a venture fund to help finance food startups,
according to the Wall Street Journal. Other large consumer
companies are doing the same. They share a motive: Growth is
increasingly hard to come by, so large companies are increasingly
looking to entrepreneurs to help them find it.
Consider the numbers. Over the last four years, the entire U.S.
grocery store’s entire food and beverage category grew just 2.3% a
year. The largest 25 food and beverage companies contributed
only 0.1% of that annual growth rate. Who drove the growth? It
came from 20,000 small companies outside of the top 100, which
together saw revenue grow by $17 billion dollars.
Despite that aggregate revenue growth, not every startup is
successful — in fact, the vast majority will fail.

Ironically, startups and established companies would both
improve their success rates if they collaborated instead of
competed. Startups and established companies bring two distinct
and equally integral skills to the table. Startups excel at giving
birth to successful proof of concepts; larger companies are much
better at successfully scaling proof of concepts.
Startups are better at detecting and unlocking emerging and
latent demand. But they often stumble at scaling their proof of
concept, not only because they’re often doing it for the first time,
but also because the skills necessary for creating are not the same
as scaling. Startups must be agile and adapt their value
proposition several times until they get it right. According to
Forbes, 58% of startups successfully figure out a clear market need
for what they have.
